title: Nvidia stock plunges 35% from record high: Is it a buying opportunity? - ​Nvidia loses over $2 trillion in market value | The Economic Times
text:
Nvidia shares have fallen around 35% from their all-time high, marking one of the steepest corrections since the artificial intelligence boom began in 2023. The chipmaker's market capitalisation has declined from nearly $5.8 trillion to approximately $3.6 trillion, wiping out more than $2 trillion in value. (Sources: Nasdaq, The Motley Fool)

The latest decline matches Nvidia's deepest sell-off since the AI investment boom gathered momentum in 2023. The previous comparable correction occurred in April 2025, when tariff-related concerns triggered a broad market sell-off and pushed Nvidia shares down by around 35%.

Investor concerns over the sustainability of massive artificial intelligence investments have put pressure on Nvidia's valuation. Markets have questioned whether hyperscalers can maintain their aggressive spending on AI infrastructure and computing capacity. However, strong demand from major technology companies continues to support Nvidia's growth outlook.

Nvidia's management has raised its revenue growth outlook for next year to 75% from an earlier projection of 70%, citing strong demand from hyperscalers. The upgraded outlook suggests that spending on AI infrastructure remains robust despite concerns over the sustainability of the investment cycle.

Wall Street analysts estimate Nvidia's revenue at $424 billion for the current fiscal year. Assuming 75% growth next year, revenue could reach approximately $742 billion. With its profit margin at around 62%, Nvidia could potentially generate $460 billion in profits, exceeding its projected revenue for the current year.

Nvidia's shares are trading at approximately nine times estimated earnings for next year, according to the article. The combination of a steep stock correction, strong AI demand and projected earnings growth could make the valuation attractive. However, concerns surrounding AI spending, leadership uncertainty and regulatory scrutiny remain important risks for investors.
